title: Candling eggs during incubation
subtitle: Candling at day 7 and day 14 shows which eggs are developing and which are not. Removing clear or dead eggs protects the developing ones.
excerpt: Candling is holding a bright light against an egg in a darkened room to see the embryo developing inside. Chicken eggs candle clearly at day 7, when the blood vessel network is visible and a dark spot shows the embryo. Clear eggs at this stage are infertile or stopped early. Day-14 candling confirms which eggs are likely to hatch.
sourceNotes: Lewis Wright, The Practical Poultry Keeper (1867), Internet Archive, chapter on incubation. University of Wisconsin Extension, incubation of poultry eggs. AHDB Poultry, incubation management guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: The pocket of air at the blunt end of an egg, visible when candling as a clear area below the shell. It grows as the egg loses moisture during incubation. An expanding air cell is a sign of correct incubation conditions.

A ring of blood visible when candling, indicating that an embryo began developing but stopped. The blood vessels, no longer used, have pooled in a ring. Remove blood-ring eggs immediately — they can explode and contaminate other eggs.

content.text: Candling on day 7 and again on day 14 removes clear and stopped eggs before they can rot or explode in the incubator. A
egg left in the incubator can contaminate 20 or 30 neighbouring eggs when it bursts. Check quickly and decisively, an egg out of the incubator for more than a few minutes loses heat.

Work in a darkened room or a dim corner. A purpose-made egg candler gives a focused bright beam that shows through the shell cleanly. A strong torch with a narrow beam works if you cup your hand around the egg and the light source.
Hold the egg at the blunt end with the candler placed against the shell. The contents should be brightly lit.

attrs.title: What you should see at day 7

content.text: Developing: a spider-web of blood vessels spreading from a small dark spot (the embryo). The
at the blunt end is distinct.
Clear (infertile): uniformly bright orange with no vessels. Remove.
Blood ring: a ring of blood with no live embryo movement. Remove immediately.
Uncertain on dark-shelled eggs: set aside and candle again at day 14.

By day 14 the embryo fills most of the egg. The contents appear dark, with the air cell clearly defined at the blunt end. You may see the chick moving inside, a small shadow shifting position, which confirms the embryo is alive.

Remove any egg that still shows a blood ring or is uniformly clear at day 14. Eggs showing a dark mass with a well-defined air cell and no smell are developing correctly. Any egg with an unpleasant smell should be removed and carefully disposed of outside.
The final week: no more candling

After day 18 on chicken eggs, stop turning and stop candling. The chick has moved into the hatching position and disturbing the egg risks displacement. Increase humidity in the incubator if you have a way to control it, and wait for the first signs of pipping, a small crack or hole in the shell.
